newsitem.title: USA: Senate rejects budget amendment, Clinton pleased.
newsitem.headline: Senate rejects budget amendment, Clinton pleased.

text.p: Senate Republicans failed Tuesday by one vote to win passage of a balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution, one of their key political goals, handing President Clinton and his Democrats an important victory.
Clinton said he was pleased with the outcome and renewed his call for the Republican majority to work with him to reach a balanced budget this year.
"Let me be clear: while I oppose a constitutional amendment, I am committed to achieving the bipartisan goal of balancing the budget by 2002," he said in a statement.

The measure failed 66-34, precisely the outcome predicted by declarations of support and opposition made in recent weeks. All 55 Republicans voted for it as did 11 Democrats, but it required a two-thirds majority of 67 to pass.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, who had made this the No. 1 issue for his party, blamed the loss on Democratic senators who he charged broke pledges made during their campaigns to vote for a balanced budget amendment.

"If we are not prepared to step up and pass this constitutional amendment now we are admitting it (balancing the budget) is not going to happen anytime soon. The deficits will build up again and again and so will the debt," the Mississippi Republican said in closing the month-long debate on the Senate floor.

Its failure in the Senate denied the budget amendment the boost House Republican leaders had said was necessary to overcome hurdles in that chamber. Nevertheless, House Majority Leader Dick Armey said it will be brought up in this congressional session.
"The House will take this up for a vote sometime this year. We will assess things as we see the outcome in the Senate," Armey, a Texas Republican, told reporters.

If changes are made in the House, particularly to ease concerns that it could harm Social Security benefits, prevent funding for long-term public works projects or endanger the economy, it might lose Republican support in the Senate, leaders said.
The balanced budget constitutional amendment has been in the works for 21 years, but came close to passage only in 1995 when it also failed by one vote.

If passed and ratified by 38 of 50 state legislatures, the amendment would require Washington to balance its budget every year during peacetime. It would take effect in 2002 or two years after ratification. Deficits would not be outlawed, but it would take a three-fifths vote, a so-called super majority, to approve deficit spending and debt increases. It would also make it harder to raise taxes.
With a look in his eye that promised political trouble in the future for Democrats, Lott told reporters before the vote the amendment would be resurrected.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle warned Lott that "playing politics" with the issue, such as bringing it up just before the 1998 congressional elections, will cost him some of the 11 Democrats who have supported the amendment.

"He shouldn't assume that simply raising this issue again at some date closer to an election, or under more politically advantageous circumstances, that somehow he's going to generate more votes," the South Dakota Democrat said.
As Daschle noted, polls showed Democrats were correct in believing the public was more concerned about security of the retirement programme than about the deficit.

Meanwhile, Republicans turned up the political heat on the White House over its fiscal 1998 budget, with leaders calling for Clinton to submit a revised plan that would meet congressional tests to produce a zero deficit in 2002.
The Congressional Budget Office reported Monday the president's plan would leave a $69 billion deficit in 2002 unless automatic spending cuts and tax increases took effect.

The White House responded that the shortfall was due to the more pessimistic economic outlook held by congressional analysts, and said its plan will balance in 2002 as promised. "The president has put his budget on the table," Office of Management and Budget director Franklin Raines said.
